articles.body:
Edson Fachin na abertura dos trabalhos do segundo semestre no STF — Foto: Gustavo Moreno/STF

O presidente do Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF), Edson Fachin, convocou o plenário da Corte para discutir na próxima terça-feira (15) relatório da Polícia Federal (PF) que apontou uma suposta relação entre o ministro Alexandre de Moraes e o ex-banqueiro Daniel Vorcaro .

Na sessão, os ministros vão discutir a validade do documento da PF feito a pedido do ministro André Mendonça.

O documento sofreu críticas de ministros da Corte. Na avaliação deles, Mendonça pediu para investigar um colega sem autorização do plenário.

Os ministros também vão decidir sobre o pedido de nulidade da Procuradoria-Geral da República (PGR) e se deve ser aberta ou arquivada investigação contra Moraes .

A PGR argumentou que Mendonça não deveria ter solicitado apuração sobre o destinatário das mensagens do ex-banqueiro, sem um pedido do Ministério Público ou da própria PF, e também que a competência para decidir sobre a eventual apuração sobre Moraes é do plenário do STF.

Na manifestação, a PGR não disse, entretanto, se as condutas apontadas pela PF poderiam representar indícios de crimes ou não.

As conversas de Vorcaro com interlocutores ocorreram por meio do aplicativo WhatsApp entre março de 2024 e agosto de 2025. O celular do dono do Master foi apreendido pela PF na Operação Compliance Zero.

Os registros estavam em um capítulo do relatório da PF dedicado a "outros encontros entre DANIEL VORCARO e ALEXANDRE DE MORAES", parte de um inquérito policial que investiga as relações e a atuação do banqueiro.

articles.title: Zema: 'uso medicinal do canabidiol não justifica liberação de drogas' | G1
articles.standfirst: Candidato a presidente pelo Novo afirmou que mudanças na política de drogas cabem ao Congresso, e não ao Judiciário, e defendeu ensino domiciliar e escolas cívico-militares.
articles.summary: Em carta a cristãos, Zema diz que uso medicinal do canabidiol não pode ser pretexto para liberar drogas, critica Judiciário e defende ensino em casa.
articles.body:
Romeu Zema, candidato do Novo à Presidência, participa de reunião com mulheres em São Paulo — Foto: Jornal Nacional/ Reprodução

O ex-governador de Minas Gerais e candidato à Presidência da República Romeu Zema (Novo) apresentou nesta quarta-feira (9) uma carta a cristãos em que afirma que o uso medicinal de substâncias como o canabidiol não pode servir de “pretexto para a liberação irresponsável das drogas”.

O documento também diz que mudanças na política de drogas devem ser decididas pelo Congresso, “e não impostas pelo Poder Judiciário”, e defende o homeschooling (ensino domiciliar) e as escolas cívico-militares.

Durante o evento de apresentação da carta, em Brasília, Zema afirmou que o Brasil vive uma crise moral e de valores.

“Fica muito claro que estamos vivendo uma crise moral no Brasil, uma de princípios e de valores. Estamos aqui exatamente por esse motivo, para deixar claro o nosso compromisso”, disse.

A carta reúne 12 compromissos assumidos por Zema e pelo candidato à vice-presidência Eduardo Girão (Novo). Veja os principais pontos:

Educação : defesa do ensino domiciliar e das escolas cívico-militares, além do direito das famílias de escolher um projeto pedagógico de acordo com suas convicções.

Aborto : oposição à ampliação das hipóteses permitidas por lei e promessa de apoio a gestantes em situação de vulnerabilidade.

Bets : compromisso de defender no Congresso uma legislação que proíba as plataformas de apostas e de restringir publicidade e patrocínios.

Drogas e segurança : oposição à flexibilização da maconha para uso recreativo e promessa de combater o crime organizado e o comércio ilegal de cigarros eletrônicos.

Supremo Tribunal Federal : promessa de enfrentar o que o documento classifica como “arbítrios da Suprema Corte”.

Receberam o documento durante o evento representantes do Fórum Nacional das Instituições Filantrópicas (Fonif), da Associação Brasileira das Instituições Evangélicas de Ensino (ABIEE), da Associação Nacional de Juristas Evangélicos (Anajure) e da Aliança Evangélica Brasileira.

Também participaram pastores de igrejas independentes, batistas, presbiterianas e pentecostais.

A carta afirma que a chapa defenderá a vida “desde a concepção até a morte” e será contrária a qualquer tentativa de ampliar as hipóteses em que o aborto é permitido.

📃 Pela lei brasileira, atualmente, o aborto é permitido em três casos: quando a gestação é decorrente de estupro; quando há risco à vida de quem gesta; e quando o feto tem anencefalia.

Na política de drogas, o documento se posiciona contra a flexibilização do consumo, do porte e do plantio de maconha para fins recreativos. Também afirma que o uso medicinal de substâncias como o canabidiol não deve servir de justificativa para uma liberação mais ampla.

“O uso medicinal de substâncias como o canabidiol (CBD) não pode ser usado como pretexto para a liberação irresponsável das drogas. Mudanças na política de drogas devem ser decididas pelo Congresso Nacional, e não impostas pelo Poder Judiciário”, diz o documento.

A carta prevê ainda a defesa da liberdade de crença e de culto e o combate à intolerância religiosa. No período eleitoral, a chapa afirma que respeitará a autonomia das igrejas e dos fiéis, sem troca de favores ou coação religiosa.

A carta defende uma legislação que proíba essas bets. A chapa promete ainda bloquear sites ilegais, restringir publicidade e patrocínios, inclusive os feitos por influenciadores, e criar políticas de prevenção e tratamento do superendividamento.

"No Executivo, atuaremos de forma célere para bloquear plataformas ilegais, restringir severamente publicidades e patrocínios (inclusive de influenciadores), responsabilizar operadores e criar políticas de prevenção e tratamento ao superendividamento", afirma a chapa no documento.

O documento também prevê ações contra o uso das apostas para lavagem de dinheiro, manipulação de resultados esportivos e financiamento do crime organizado, mas não detalha quais serão as medidas a serem aplicadas.

No último ponto, dedicado às liberdades civis, a chapa promete uma postura “firme e institucional” diante do que classifica como “arbítrios da Suprema Corte e de qualquer instituição do sistema de Justiça”.

O documento afirma que as liberdades de imprensa, expressão, pensamento, associação e partidária terão “atenção especial” em um eventual governo.

articles.title: Bebê nasce em ambulância no trajeto de hospital em Presidente Prudente | G1
articles.standfirst: Equipe do Same foi acionada para atender uma gestante em trabalho de parto na manhã desta terça-feira (8). Mãe e bebê foram encaminhados ao Hospital Estadual após o primeiro atendimento.
articles.summary: Um bebê nasceu dentro de uma ambulância do Serviço de Atendimento Móvel de Emergência (Same), em Presidente Prudente (SP), na manhã desta terça-feira (8).
articles.body:
Profissionais do Same de Presidente Prudente (SP) realizaram parto dentro de ambulância nesta terça-feira (9) — Foto: Prefeitura de Presidente Prudente/Divulgação

Um bebê nasceu dentro de uma ambulância do Serviço de Atendimento Móvel de Emergência (Same), em Presidente Prudente (SP), na manhã desta terça-feira (8).

De acordo com a prefeitura, a equipe havia sido acionada às 6h05 para atender a uma gestante de 40 semanas em trabalho de parto.

Quando os profissionais chegaram ao local, encontraram a mulher em pé, no portão da casa. Durante a avaliação inicial, ela apresentava contrações de forte intensidade, perda de líquido e o bebê já estava em coroamento, ou seja, quando a cabeça começa a aparecer no momento do parto.

Diante da situação, considerada de parto iminente, a mulher foi imediatamente colocada dentro da ambulância e acomodada para receber atendimento. Os profissionais realizaram o parto dentro da própria viatura.

Após o nascimento, a equipe prestou os primeiros cuidados à mãe e ao bebê. Os dois foram encaminhados ao Hospital Estadual, onde passaram por avaliação médica e receberam atendimento pós-parto.

A ocorrência contou com a atuação do médico Thiago, do enfermeiro Reginaldo Joerke, do técnico em enfermagem Marcos e do condutor Reginaldo.

Segundo a Prefeitura de Presidente Prudente, mãe e bebê passam bem.

articles.summary: Professora Maria do Carmo, candidata ao Governo do Amazonas, defende investimentos em estradas e transporte fluvial para melhorar a logística e o escoamento no estado.
articles.body:
Professora Maria do Carmo defende integração de rios e estradas para garantir logística no AM — Foto: Reprodução/TV A Crítica

A candidata ao Governo do Amazonas, Professora Maria do Carmo (PL), participou de uma entrevista em uma emissora de TV na manhã desta terça-feira (8), em Manaus . Durante a conversa, ela respondeu a perguntas de estudantes e apresentou propostas para melhorar a logística no interior do estado.

Professora Maria do Carmo disputa o cargo pela coligação "Mudar é Urgente", formada pelo Partido Liberal (PL). Ela já concorreu a outros cargos. Em 2024, foi candidata a vice-prefeita de Manaus na chapa de Capitão Alberto Neto (PL). Em 2022, concorreu ao cargo de suplente do então candidato Arthur Neto (PSDB).

Questionada sobre como garantir o abastecimento dos municípios durante períodos de seca extrema, a candidata defendeu uma logística integrada entre o transporte fluvial e o rodoviário. Segundo Maria do Carmo, é necessário investir na recuperação e construção de estradas para ampliar as alternativas de deslocamento e o escoamento de mercadorias no interior do estado.

"Ela não pode ser só o rio, porque o rio tem seus problemas também", afirmou a candidata, que também defendeu a realização de dragagens em trechos onde a medida for possível.

Como exemplo, a candidata citou a estrada que liga os municípios de Apuí e Novo Aripuanã, com cerca de 293 quilômetros, além de outros trechos rodoviários que, segundo ela, poderiam fortalecer a conexão entre cidades do interior e reduzir a dependência exclusiva dos rios para o transporte.

A agenda da candidata nesta quarta-feira (9) inclui ainda outros compromissos na capital amazonense. À tarde, Maria do Carmo realizará gravações para o programa eleitoral. Em seguida, participa de atendimento interno com lideranças da capital.

articles.standfirst: Em decisão liminar, Dino diz que houve invasão de atribuições do plenário e desfez afastamento de delegados da cúpula da PF que havia sido determinado por André Mendonça.
articles.summary: Em meio à crise no STF, Flávio Dino reverteu o afastamento de delegados da PF e André Mendonça cobrou providências imediatas do ministro Luiz Edson Fachin.
articles.body:
A guerra de liminares no Supremo Tribunal Federal ( STF ) ampliou a pressão para que o presidente da Corte, Luiz Edson Fachin , anuncie alguma medida concreta para tentar conter a crise.

Ministros procuraram Fachin, por telefone, logo após a decisão de Flávio Dino que desfez o afastamento do diretor-geral da Polícia Federal , Andrei Rodrigues, e do diretor de inteligência, Leandro Almada, que havia sido determinado pelo colega André Mendonça .

Um desses contatos, conforme apurou a TV Globo , foi feito pelo próprio ministro André Mendonça, que, na ligação, chamou a decisão de Dino de "ilegal" e cobrou providências .

Há também previsão de que o presidente do STF receba ainda nesta quarta o ministro Alexandre de Moraes , que é vice-presidente da Corte e um dos protagonistas da crise Master no Supremo.

Na avaliação de magistrados ouvidos de forma reservada, Fachin precisa assumir o controle da crise e adotar uma providência para frear ações das alas de Moraes e Mendonça .

Nos bastidores, há o entendimento de que os dois grupos atropelaram e tentaram esvaziar as prerrogativas de Fachin .

Na decisão que colocou Andrei de volta no cargo, Dino afirmou que Mendonça invadiu atribuições e não aguardou decisão de Fachin ou do plenário sobre os relatórios da PF:

um que apontou suposta relação de Moraes e o ex-banqueiro Daniel Vorcaro; e

o outro, de inteligência e sem valor probatório, que questionou a condução de inquéritos do INSS e Master por Mendonça.

Pressionado e em meio a uma crise sem precedentes no STF, Fachin cancelou a sessão plenária da Corte que estava agendada para esta quarta-feira (9).

articles.title: Reporter’s Notebook: 9/11 is just a history chapter for a new generation of Americans
articles.summary: A quarter century after 9/11, one-third of Americans alive that day are gone, and the memories of Sept. 11, 2001, grow increasingly faded.
articles.body: It’s faded. Not from decay. Not from neglect. It’s simply the passage of time. The memories are vague. Elusive. Distant. And some who lived it are simply no longer here. Roughly one-third of all Americans who were alive on 9/11 aren’t around anymore to observe the 25th anniversary of that abominable day. And so the recollections of Sept. 11, 2001, are diluted. NEW 9/11 MUSEUM EXHIBIT AIMS TO CONNECT YOUNGER AMERICANS TO THE ATTACKS THROUGH POWERFUL ARTIFACTS To some, Sept. 11 is just another day. But it’s something different for those who weren’t around to live and breathe the horror. To many, 9/11 is like Pearl Harbor Day. Lots of people know about it. They understand it’s what triggered the U.S.’s entry into World War II. But they can’t quite explain much more. The same with other historical-shifting moments. Aug. 6 and 9, 1945 — the days the U.S. bombed Hiroshima and Nagasaki, effectively ending World War II. Nov. 22, 1963 — the day a gunman mowed down President John F. Kennedy Jr. in Dallas. A lot of people remember the Space Shuttle Challenger exploding. But few could tell you that it happened on Jan. 28, 1986. The quintessence of 9/11 is the date. Kind of like July 4th. A bit like Jan. 6 and the Capitol riot. However, we were told on Sept. 11, 2001, that things would never be the same. But how can those who didn’t experience it understand what "the same" was like if they never lived it? Just last month, a relative of mine who soon turns 26 asked, "What it was like to fly before 9/11?" I can regale you with stories about myself and a rag-tag group of high school friends, driving to the Cincinnati airport, clearing security and just wandering around the Delta gates, "hanging out" back in the mid-1980s. No ticket. No questions asked. Just a visit to Cinnabon. But the "before times" question about 9/11 is a broader conversation. It’s not just about "what changed" when you take off your shoes and bustle through security to fly. LIZ PEEK: WE CANNOT LET THE LEFT REWRITE WHAT HAPPENED ON 9/11 A nine-and-a-half-foot-tall plaque hangs in the East Front vestibule of the U.S. Capitol near the Rotunda. It commemorates Flight 93, which crashed near Shanksville, Pa., on 9/11. It took a few years, but the U.S. intelligence services finally determined that the fourth plane was bound for the U.S. Capitol. That’s where Todd Beamer and a cadre of everyday Americans voted (mind you, at 35,000 feet) to commandeer a drinks cart and rush the cockpit in an effort to seize control of the plane. "Let’s roll!" Beamer was overheard saying on a cellphone as they charged down the aisle. That two-word phrase became a battle cry for a nation as it waged the war on terrorism. The Boeing 757 hurtled toward Washington at 563 mph. It was 20 minutes out from the federal city when the plane crashed, upside down, in the Pennsylvania countryside. Shanksville is now one of those places forever notched into American history. A place not as famous, say, as Gettysburg or Jamestown, but not a footnote, either. Shanksville is part of the vernacular like Shiloh, Seneca Falls, Kent. People might know that something historic happened there. But they aren’t exactly sure what. Scores of markers dot the U.S. Capitol, denoting important things from yesteryear. Wander into Statuary Hall in the Capitol and you’ll find the desk locations of eight presidents who served in the House. But the spot where President Franklin Pierce once sat just seems like an historical annotation. Pierce toiled there nearly two centuries ago. And he’s hardly prominent among American chief executives. There’s a plaque just outside the Old Supreme Court chamber. It tells the story of how Samuel B. Morse sent the first electronic message from that room to Baltimore over a wire in 1844. "What hath God wrought!" reads the plaque, commemorating Morse’s transmission. That event christened the age of near-instant communication – now ubiquitous in the form of news alerts and TikTok videos appearing instantly in the palms of our hands. But that plaque in the Capitol’s East Front vestibule doesn’t memorialize something that happened there. It marks something that didn’t happen there. The plaque reads that the actions of the 40 passengers and crew "not only saved countless lives, but may have saved the U.S. Capitol from destruction." In other words, this global citadel to democracy with its ivory dome might not pierce the Washington skyline were it not for a plane that crashed 167 miles away. Shanksville. Shiloh. Seneca Falls. Kent. TRUMP CONFIRMS PENTAGON PLANS FOR 25TH ANNIVERSARY OF 9/11 ATTACKS, DISPUTES REPORT ON GROUND ZERO ABSENCE I’ve driven the Pennsylvania Turnpike past Somerset for decades now. That’s where the signs direct you north 10 miles to the Flight 93 National Memorial. I budgeted time into my travels to visit the memorial on one frigid, windy morning a few Februarys ago. Inside, you stand at a vista, staring downhill into a small ravine and tree line where the plane crashed. On that morning, I couldn’t help but notice there was no wildlife to be seen or heard. No deer. No birds chirping. A disturbing silence. Perhaps it was the billowing wind of that frosty morning. Maybe the snow. But I noticed no footprints gouging the crisp snowpack. It was almost as though the animals were aware of something. Dare I say understood what happened in this field a quarter-century ago. Perhaps the local fauna stayed hushed out of reverence for those who perished. A tribute to their heroism, saving the U.S. Capitol. Or perhaps it was something else. Maybe the creatures were so reserved because of the malevolence which was also on board Flight 93. One can only speculate that the animals remain hushed because of the peculiar unease enveloping the place. Even on a crisp but blustery winter morning. Shanksville is a burial ground. And in a few more decades or even a hundred years, those who visit there will walk the paths or peer out over the panorama, trying to grasp the scope of what unfolded there on 9/11. FOX NEWS MEDIA ANNOUNCES EXTENSIVE 9/11 ANNIVERSARY COVERAGE FROM GROUND ZERO, PENTAGON AND SHANKSVILLE You can visit Gettysburg and Antietam and do that now. But much is left to the imagination. Perhaps embroidered by what was picked up in a history class. Augmented by a marker or description on a bronze plaque. In another quarter-century, there will be even fewer people around who remember 9/11. Another 25 after that and many of those still living might be infirm. Confined to wheelchairs. The final generation of messengers who can speak firsthand about what happened that day. Kind of like when honor flights descend on Washington to visit the World War II Memorial on the National Mall. It’s just the passage of time. The plaque inside the Capitol will continue to tell the story. And in many ways, just the fact that the Capitol remains standing tells the story, too. Its presence attests to the bravery that manifested itself somewhere over eastern Ohio and is interred in a western Pennsylvania clearing. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP We know this now. Even though some of what we recall is faded. But the memories and understanding of the significance will naturally calcify. Details will grow hazy. People will know the date 9/11. But it may just be that — a date. Like Pearl Harbor Day. President Franklin Delano Roosevelt referred to Dec. 7, 1941, as "a date which will live infamy." 9/11 will live in infamy. But it’s unclear how that date will live in the minds of Americans.

articles.title: Fmr Biden ambassador blames Trump for Canada playing 'footsie' with China
articles.summary: Former U.S. Ambassador David L. Cohen says Canada is playing "footsie" with China on trade as Trump's hardline policies push allies toward new deals.
articles.body: Former U.S. Ambassador to Canada David L. Cohen is blaming the Trump administration's hardline trade pressure for pushing Ottawa into engaging with China. "I think Canada has tentatively tried to play some footsie with China that the Trump administration may not be happy with," Cohen, who served as President Joe Biden’s ambassador to Canada from 2021 to 2025, said in an interview with Fox News Digital. "There is a discomfort with that," Cohen says, while arguing that it is ultimately Canada's reflex to sentiment against President Donald Trump – particularly his hardline trade policies and rhetoric about the neighbor to the north being a "51st state." VANCE SAYS CANADA FRIENDLIER TO CHINA ON TRADE THAN TO US: 'INSANITY' "One of downsides of the aggressive Trump administration treatment of Canada and many other allies and partners is that the irony is that those policies are pushing those countries to at least consider broader and larger deals with China, which of course is wholly inconsistent with a major thrust of President Trump's international trade policy," Cohen continued. "So, how that shakes out, it's all a matter of degree and balance. "But I think there's no doubt that the aggressiveness of the Trump administration positions has caused many countries to at least reevaluate whether there are additional deals that can be made with China." The comments come as U.S.-Canada trade tensions spiral after negotiations collapsed last month. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney on Tuesday accused Washington of seeking dependence rather than partnership. "The most fundamental issue is that the cumulative U.S. demands revealed that they wanted us to become even more reliant on them, not less," Carney said. "In too many areas, they wanted dependency, not a true economic partnership." TRUMP TAUNTS CANADA ON RENAMING LAKE ONTARIO THE 'LAKE AMERICA' AMID RISING BORDER TRADE RIFT Notably, the fallout comes just weeks before Chinese dictator Xi Jinping makes an historic trip to the White House to talk trade – something that never happened during the Biden administration despite Biden's onetime quip before the COVID-19 pandemic that "China's not bad folks." Vice President JD Vance, speaking in Maine last month, accused Canada of giving Chinese goods better treatment than products from American northern border states. "They treat Chinese goods more fairly than they do the goods that come from the people of Maine: It’s insanity," Vance said. "And what we’ve said to Canada is, ‘Stop it.’" Cohen, however, was careful not to cast Canada as blameless in the trade feud. He admitted U.S. dairy farmers have legitimate complaints about Canada’s tariff-rate quota system, saying the issue has frustrated administrations of both parties for years. WHITE HOUSE EXPOSES ‘TRANSSHIPMENT SCAM’ COSTING US UP TO $26B, POINTS FINGER AT CHINA "This is one of the totally legitimate trade issues that exists between the United States and Canada," Cohen said. "There is contention there that is hurting American dairy farmers. Yes, I will be honest and clear about that." "That tension existed under Joe Biden. Was he able to solve that problem? No," he added. "It was something that was discussed and discussed more than once. We just never got there." Cohen, supportive of Trump's "substance" on trade talks but not the "style," did credit Trump for replacing NAFTA with the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement, calling USMCA a "terrific deal" that improved continental trade. TRUMP TRADE CHIEF WARNS CANADA WALKED AWAY FROM 'THE BEST DEAL' TO TRIGGER 50% U.S. TARIFFS "I gave President Trump a lot of credit for that because it was a much better deal than NAFTA," Cohen said. "I think he deserves credit for that." "I do push back at times on some of the rhetoric that President Trump has chosen to use, not necessarily the substance, but maybe the style that he sometimes uses to pursue his substance," he added. "There are such fundamental differences on the substance of President Trump’s trade policy that I think the treatment of President Trump is different than the treatment of President Biden," Cohen observed. "But when professional negotiators were in the room, they seemed to have been making a lot of progress." Cohen believes the two sides need to return to professional negotiators, arguing that U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer and Canadian officials had shown they could discuss difficult issues before the talks broke down. TRUMP MUST CLOSE THE BACK DOOR CHINA USES TO EXPLOIT NORTH AMERICAN TRADE "I have an enormous amount of respect for U.S. Trade Representative Greer," Cohen said. "He is the ultimate professional trade negotiator, which is why he’s in that job. He didn’t get there by accident. President Trump put him in that job." By contrast, Cohen said Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick – who was on the call that Friday night in August when talks broke down at the 11th hour – needs to stay in his lane. "Secretary of Commerce Lutnick, with all due respect, is not a professional negotiator," Cohen said. "That’s not the Commerce secretary’s job. It’s USTR’s job to negotiate trade deals with other countries." Lutnick has suggested in interviews about the infamous breakdown in talks that Canadians' politics are at play in keeping Carney from cutting a deal with Trump, a man the provincial leaders and Canadian public have long been disenchanted with. TRUMP TRADE CHIEF REVEALS WHAT PRECEDED CANADA WALKING AWAY FROM 'BEST DEAL IN THE WORLD' "Friday at 4 o'clock, the Canadians call: They start adding crazy ideas to the mix," Lutnick said recently. "So, I said to one of the ministers, 'Are you actually trying to blow this up?' And his answer to me was, 'I'm not allowed to say that.' And they blew it up for political reasons only." Cohen said of Lutnick's account that "until proven otherwise, I take every senior government official at his word, period," and that he has "no way of knowing whether that is true or not." But, he admitted, Carney taking the nearly finished trade deal back to the provinces did not go over well – particularly amid his rising popularity among Canadians for being an anti-Trump force – because "the premiers of the provinces have more sway in federal policy than most governors do in federal policy." CANADIAN PM TELLS TRUMP TO 'STOP TRYING TO BE TOUGH' IN TRADE FIGHT "It appears that Canada made the decision that the deal that was being offered was not a deal that they could accept," Cohen said. "He may have made a judgment that although he and his team had pushed this deal as far as they could, and that it was, in his eyes, as good a deal as he was going to get at that point, that he could not sell that politically in Canada." "That’s not the same as saying that he was walking away for political reasons," Cohen added. "It’s just the nature of a big, complex negotiation." TRUMP'S CANADA TARIFF FIGHT REACHES CRITICAL POINT AS HOUSE GOP SUMMONS TRADE CHIEF Ultimately, Cohen said the breakdown between the closest allies and trade partners in the world will be a story long told. "There are going to be books written about what caused the negotiations to fall apart," he said. "But independent of all the dialogue about that: There is no dispute that these professional negotiators were able to have a civil relationship and talk about really different difficult substantive issues out of the eyes and the ears of the press and with full respect for each other and for the countries. That's my vision for the way in which trade negotiations should occur and they did occur – and it was a two-way street." "You can’t make a deal if you’re not talking to each other," Cohen said. "Of that, I am 100% certain."

articles.title: Proposal would pay homeowners 'data center dividends' to counter growing backlash
articles.summary: Think tank proposes sharing data center tax revenue with local residents through direct payments, tax credits or scholarships
articles.body: As opposition to artificial intelligence data centers spreads across rural America, one group is proposing "data center dividends" to counter the backlash by allowing residents to share directly in the wealth generated by the technology hubs. A new report from the Bitcoin Policy Institute, a think tank based in Washington, D.C., proposes that data center dividends are a model that would return part of the property tax revenue generated by AI data centers directly to households living in the communities that host the data centers, potentially providing annual payments of between about $4,500 and $8,900 per household without creating new taxes or increasing costs for developers. "Every American deserves to benefit from the AI boom," Sam Lyman, head of research at the nonprofit, told Fox News Digital. "It can't just be the developers in Silicon Valley who are becoming wealthy from this revolution. It needs to be the Americans who are building the county infrastructure that makes these data centers possible in the first place." The proposal comes as opposition to data centers intensifies nationwide, fomented over the past year by a network of socialists and communist nonprofits funded by a tech tycoon, Neville Roy Singham, living in Shanghai, supporting the Chinese Communist Party and a "new world order" promulgated by Chinese leader Xi Jinping. The opposition has widened to conservatives and centrists, with the report noting that Americans are now more likely to oppose a data center in their community than a nuclear power plant. In a poll earlier this year, Gallup found that 71% of Americans oppose construction of an AI data center in their area, while only 53% oppose a nearby nuclear plant. The report says local data center moratoriums have exploded from six in 2024 to 59 last year and 294 last month. Over the past year, groups in the Singham network – including the Party for Socialism and Liberation, the People's Forum, CodePink and BreakThrough News – have opposed data centers and also Flock surveillance cameras with aggressive media campaigns, elevating China as a technological powerhouse and denigrating any developments by U.S. technology companies. "These influence actions are cognitive warfare. Foreign actors don't need Americans to become pro-China," Rob Joyce, former director of cybersecurity at the National Security Agency, recently told Fox News Digital. "They need Americans to argue for the outcomes Beijing wants. And a free society that can't build the power and govern the advanced technology is going to wind up renting it from the adversary, read the PRC, that doesn't share its own values. And that scares me as an American." Lyman said the political problem is that many Americans believe technology companies are reaping the benefits of the AI boom while local communities bear the costs. The propaganda campaigns by the pro-China groups are promoting that message by describing tech executives as "oligarchs" and "imperialists." One constant message in the campaigns is "People Over Profits." "I really think that data center dividends will reverse the momentum in the data center debate, because suddenly every American who lives in these counties where data centers might be built recognizes that he or she can have a material stake in the AI economy," said Lyman, a former senior advisor and speechwriter for Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent. Polling cited in the report found that 73% of Americans believe the costs of data center construction outweigh the benefits, while voters overwhelmingly believe AI will primarily enrich executives and business owners rather than workers. Rather than creating a new tax, the proposal would redirect a portion of property tax revenue that counties already collect from data centers. "Data center dividends can ensure that rural Americans rise in the age of AI alongside the engineers developing this technology," the report notes. Under the model, counties would first continue funding schools, roads, police and other essential services. After those obligations are met, local communities would return a portion of remaining revenue directly to residents through annual checks, direct deposits, tax credits, utility bill credits or permanent investment funds. The report emphasizes that the dividends would be financed entirely from existing tax revenue, meaning developers wouldn't pay any additional taxes. The report estimates that a single one-gigawatt AI data center could generate enough tax revenue to provide households in a typical rural county between $4,500 and $8,900 annually in a "data center dividend," depending on how much revenue local governments dedicate to dividends after paying for public services. The estimate is based on tax collections from Loudoun County, Va., one of the nation's largest data center hubs. Loudoun collected about $685 million in personal property taxes on data center computer equipment in fiscal year 2024. Dividing those collections by the county's data center electrical load produced an estimate of roughly $165 million in annual property tax revenue per gigawatt of AI infrastructure, researchers estimated. The report cites new policies in West Feliciana Parish, La., where policymakers are attempting to spread new-found wealth. The parish expects a Hut 8 AI campus to generate about $90 million annually, more than tripling its current budget, according to estimates. Earlier this year, Louisiana lawmakers passed Act 434, allowing local officials to provide property tax credits funded by the new revenue, although lawmakers removed an earlier proposal that would have authorized direct cash payments. If the cash provision had remained, the report estimates households could have received about $5,600 annually if one-quarter of the revenue were distributed, or $11,200 annually if half the revenue were shared with residents after funding government services. In another example, Alaska has a "Permanent Fund," or state-owned investment account that collects part of Alaska's revenues from oil produced on state land, invests it in stocks, bonds and real estate, and disburses part of the returns to residents as an annual dividend. The report outlines several options communities could adopt. Lyman argues that direct payments create stronger public support than simply lowering taxes or expanding government spending because residents would see the benefit. "I think a lot that opposition is born from the fact that many Americans feel left out of the AI boom. They feel like this economic revolution is taking place without them," said Lyman, noting, "What data center dividends do... is they give every American in rural America a share in the material prosperity that is taking place with artificial intelligence." The report notes that rural counties possess two scarce assets essential for AI development – land and abundant power – and argues those communities should share directly in the economic gains generated by the AI buildout. articles.title: 'Gambling with our lives': AI researcher quits Anthropic
articles.summary: An artificial intelligence researcher who left OpenAI to join Anthropic has decided to leave the industry, accusing both US companies of "gambling with our l...
articles.body:
An artificial intelligence researcher who left OpenAI to join Anthropic has decided to leave the industry, accusing both US companies of "gambling with our lives" in the race to develop AI models capable of self-improvement.

Jacob Coxon, 27, spent the past three years pretraining AI models, first at OpenAI and then, this year, at its rival Anthropic, which he considered more cautious in its approach.

Pretraining is the stage where AI models absorb vast quantities of data.

"Neither company is acting responsibly. They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives," Coxon said on Tuesday.

"The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade," he said in a post on X.

"This is not a marketing stunt," he added.

Superintelligence is the theoretical point when AI's capabilities exceed human intelligence.

Anthropic safety executive Evan Hubinger backed up Coxon on X.

"We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!" he said, adding that he estimated that risk at more than 10 percent over the next decade.

Hubinger said Anthropic is "trying its best", but does not yet have a plan to ensure an AI system that surpasses human capabilities would obey its creators. He said there was a "low" risk of that happening with current models.

Coxon's resignation comes as Anthropic prepares for its market debut, following a summer marked by unauthorized hacks carried out by AI tools during testing.

The two companies did not immediately respond to AFP requests for comment.

AI leaders say so-called "recursive self-improvement," a stage where AI systems could essentially design and train the next generation of AI with little human involvement, is drawing near.

Coxon considers Anthropic's efforts genuine but said he believes no company can responsibly develop an AI that surpasses humans without government intervention or a coordinated slowdown.

"At Anthropic, the stakes are well-understood, but they are locked in a race to get there first -- they believe no one else will act responsibly, so they must do it themselves, despite the risk," he said.

In February, Anthropic removed a pledge from its safety charter to halt the development of its models if it failed to control their risks.

It argued that if it unilaterally paused its work, its less cautious rivals would dominate the industry, making it less safe overall.

At the end of July, more than 1,000 tech industry employees, including Anthropic's CEO Dario Amodei, called on Washington to support a coordinated slowdown in the development of the most advanced AI systems.

OpenAI halted training of its latest models for two weeks in August before resuming it under tighter controls.

On Sunday, OpenAI's chief scientist, Jakub Pachocki, called for "extreme caution."

"International coordination on future AI development needs to become a top priority for governments around the world," he said in a blog post.

AI models are not regulated by federal law in the United States.

In September, Senator Bernie Sanders and Democratic Representative Greg Casar introduced a bill seeking to suspend AI development until a federal regulator is created.

articles.title: Trump gave $45,000 cash gifts to Natalie Harp and two other aides, public records show
articles.summary: The White House has described the $45,000 cash gifts to Natalie Harp and three others as personal - and legal.
articles.body:
President Donald Trump gave sizable cash gifts to four White House staffers, including $45,000 (£33,000) to his close aide Natalie Harp, financial disclosures released by his administration show.

Two staff members got the same amount as Harp, while his longtime aide and director of Oval Office Operations Walt Nauta, received $22,000.

No other White House staffer has declared any gifts from the president, the documents show. Federal employees are prohibited from receiving outside compensation for their duties.

The White House has described the gifts as personal in nature, unrelated to the staffers' work and legal under US law.

In a statement provided to the BBC, a White House official said that the president "has a longstanding practice of giving Christmas gifts to people in his orbit, including at times employees and aides, both in government and in his time in the private sector".

"The gifts at issue here have nothing to do with any of these individuals' official government duties, and are entirely permissible under relevant legal and ethical standards," the official added.

The cash gifts, totalling $157,000, are marked as a "cash gift for the holidays" for Nauta, Harp and two other officials: communications advisor Margo Martin and Chamberlain Harris, a White House aide who serves as Trump's executive assistant.

The White House did not answer a separate query from the BBC on why the other 91 listed staff members did not receive gifts.

The four recipients of the cash gifts are among those widely considered as close to the US president.

Harp, 35, is among Trump's longest-serving and most loyal aides. She is often trusted with typing out his frequent Truth Social posts, among other responsibilities.

Last month, she was thrust into the national spotlight after she was named as one of a small number of people who stayed with Trump as he secretly swapped planes leaving Turkey last month.

Nauta, a US Navy veteran, has also long been at Trump's side. He served as a White House military valet to the president in his first term, and later joined him as an assistant at his Mar-a-Lago estate in Florida after he left office.

In June 2023, he was indicted alongside Trump on charges that he mishandled national security documents. The case was ultimately dismissed.

The third recipient, Margo Martin, is well known for documenting Trump's activities on social media.

While the final recipient, 26-year-old Chamberlain Harris, officially serves as the president's executive assistant. In February, he was also appointed to the US Commission of Fine Arts which oversees the construction of the White House ballroom and other Trump-directed projects in Washington.

Cassandra Burke Roberston, a law professor and director of the Center for Professional Ethics at Case Western Reserve University in Ohio, told the BBC that "it's not an easy call" to say whether the cash gifts were ethical or not.

Robertson noted that the compensation amounts "seem to be standard" based on their employee level.

"That suggests that the decision on how much to give was made on the basis of somebody's employment situation," she said. "And not their state of friendship with the president."

Additionally, Robertson said that even if legal, the gifts - along with recent controversies involving prediction markets and cryptocurrencies - could raise eyebrows among the public.

"It does add to a generalised perception of really rampant conflicts of interest," she said.

There are no other known instances of a serving US president giving cash gifts to staffers at the White House.

Many presidents, however, have given souvenirs or personal mementos to staff.

President Barack Obama, for example, gave former press secretary Robert Gibbs a framed necktie that he had once borrowed ahead of the Democratic National Convention in 2004.

articles.title: Jackson, El-Sayed hold slight edge in key Senate races: CNN poll
articles.summary: A new poll found Democratic Senate nominees Troy Jackson and Abdul El-Sayed holding slight leads in their respective races, with less than two months before Election Day. The CNN/SSRS survey, released Wednesday, found that 48 percent of 880 registered voters in Maine backed Jackson, while 45 percent said they will vote for five-term incumbent Sen.…
articles.body:
A new poll found Democratic Senate nominees Troy Jackson and Abdul El-Sayed holding slight leads in their respective races , with less than two months before Election Day.

The CNN/SSRS survey , released Wednesday, found that 48 percent of 880 registered voters in Maine backed Jackson, while 45 percent said they will vote for five-term incumbent Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine). Another 4 percent said they would vote for neither candidate, while 3 percent backed another candidate.

Of the 839 Mainers who voiced support for a candidate, 82 percent said their mind is already made up. Roughly 18 percent of the remainder acknowledged they could change their mind while the rest did not pick a candidate, according to the poll.

Jackson’s lead over Collins was within the margin of error of 3.7 percentage points. The Democrat most recently was the president of the Maine Senate for six years, a tenure ending in 2024.

As for El-Sayed, a progressive and former Wayne County, Mich., health official, led former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.) by 3 points in the CNN poll, with 47 percent support to the GOP candidate’s 44 percent.

Five percent of the 843 respondents backed neither candidate, while 3 percent said they will vote for someone else in the Wolverine State. El-Sayed’s lead, like that of Jackson, was within the margin of error of 4.1 percentage points.

A larger share of likely Michigan voters could be persuaded, the survey shows. More than a quarter of those who already picked a candidate said they either could change their mind or have not yet picked a candidate.

El-Sayed and Rogers are battling to succeed outgoing Sen. Gary Peters (D), who has represented Michigan in the upper chamber for two terms. While a Republican has not won a Senate race in the state since former Sen. Spencer Abraham in 1994, President Trump won Michigan in two of his three presidential runs.

The Maine and Michigan races are crucial in the fight for Senate control, as Democrats need to pick up a net of four seats to retake the upper chamber.

As of Tuesday, Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ) gave Jackson and El-Sayed a 53 percent and 66 percent chance to win their races, respectively.

DDHQ gives Democrats a slightly better than 50-50 shot to win the Senate, a shift from late July — when it gave Republicans a 6 in 10 chance at maintaining control.

articles.title: Missouri Supreme Court threatens secretary of state with contempt amid intensifying redistricting battle
articles.summary: Secretary of State Denny Hoskins must appear Thursday to explain why he shouldn't be held in contempt over Missouri's congressional maps battle.
articles.body: The Missouri Supreme Court signaled Tuesday that it was considering holding Secretary of State Denny Hoskins in contempt amid an escalating battle over proposed congressional maps. Hoskins, a Republican, said Tuesday that he would keep using the congressional districts redrawn last year, despite a U.S. Supreme Court decision that left standing a state Supreme Court order requiring Missouri to use its old districts instead. "I look forward to my day in court," Hoskins said in a post on X that cited the supremacy clause of the U.S. Constitution. MISSOURI AG FILES PETITION ASKING SUPREME COURT TO REVIVE TRUMP-BACKED REDISTRICTING MAP Hoskins must appear in court Thursday to explain why he shouldn't be held in contempt for instructing election officials to use the 2025 congressional map despite an injunction barring its use. Last week, Missouri's high court ruled that the map backed by President Donald Trump cannot be used because thousands of voters signed a petition demanding a statewide referendum on it. SUPREME COURT DEALS BLOW TO VIRGINIA DEMOCRATS IN FIGHT OVER STATE COURT ELECTION MAP RULING Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh declined to grant an emergency stay requested by Hoskins, leaving in place the injunction ordered by the state Supreme Court. However, shortly after Kavanaugh's announcement, U.S. District Judge Stephen Clark, a Trump appointee, issued a temporary restraining order prohibiting Missouri from using any map other than the new 2025 districts. GEORGIA REDISTRICTING BATTLE REVIVED AFTER APPEALS COURT OVERTURNS FEDERAL COURT DECISION Opponents of the new redistricting plan quickly filed a notice to appeal Clark's order to the 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals. "An individual federal judge cannot overrule the Missouri Supreme Court," said attorney Chuck Hatfield, who represents People Not Politicians, the group that sponsored the referendum petition. RNC AND NRCC FILE LAWSUIT DEFENDING MISSOURI'S NEW CONGRESSIONAL MAP AGAINST DEMOCRATIC CHALLENGES Missouri Attorney General Catherine Hanaway said she was prepared to comply with Clark's order, which she argued "binds the state to using" the new congressional districts. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "We maintain that changing the congressional map in between the primary and general elections is simply not feasible and profoundly unjust to Missouri voters," she wrote on X. BLOCKBUSTER SUPREME COURT VOTING RIGHTS RULING IGNITES REDISTRICTING WAR ACROSS SOUTHERN STATES The conflict is part of a broader, nationwide effort by Republicans to redraw congressional districts mid-decade to gain U.S. House seats. Missouri currently has six Republicans and two Democrats in the U.S. House. The new redistricting plan would eliminate one Democratic seat, currently held by Rep. Emanuel Cleaver.

articles.title: Associated Press will stick with Lake Ontario over Trump’s renamed ‘Lake America’
articles.summary: The Associated Press will continue to refer to Lake Ontario by its original name, despite President Trump’s push to rename the body of water “Lake America.” The president signed an executive order last month directing the name change, marking the latest in his efforts to rename geographical places like the Gulf of Mexico. The order…
articles.body:
The Associated Press will continue to refer to Lake Ontario by its original name, despite President Trump’s push to rename the body of water “Lake America.”

The president signed an executive order last month directing the name change, marking the latest in his efforts to rename geographical places like the Gulf of Mexico. The order came amid his administration’s ongoing trade fight with Canada.

The AP has instructed its reporters to refer to the body of water as Lake Ontario and note the president’s new name if relevant to the story, according to guidance shared by the news organization on Wednesday.

AP reporters were provided a statement to include in their coverage to explain the outlet’s decision.

“The Associated Press will refer to Lake Ontario by its original name, including the name Trump has chosen when relevant,” the statement said. “As a global news agency that disseminates news around the world, the AP must ensure that place names and geography are recognizable to broad audiences.”

The AP noted in the guidance to its newsroom that Trump’s executive order only requires the U.S. government to refer to the lake by the new name and that Canada and other countries have publicly stated they will not adopt the new name.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney pushed back on the proposed name change, pointing to its Indigenous history in a social media post following the executive order’s enactment.

“We know that America is changing. Their trading relationships, their foreign policies, their national monuments, their hydronyms,” Carney wrote. “Canadians also know that naming reality means calling it Lake Ontario — then, now and always.”

Last year, the AP made a similar decision regarding the president’s push to rename the Gulf of Mexico as the “Gulf of America.” The White House responded by blocking AP reporters from attending events.

Popular apps Google Maps and Apple Maps changed their labels on the water body for U.S. users to comply with the president’s renaming push. Interior Secretary Doug Burgum told Fox News recently that Trump “reached out to Apple directly” to request the change.

MapQuest, which was one of the few map services to refuse the proposed change, said it saw a surge in downloads after the company announced it would keep the name as Lake Ontario. The app also previously refused the president’s push to rename the Gulf of Mexico.

“We took the same approach we did with the Gulf of Mexico: be part of the conversation, and give people an app that keeps the names they’re familiar with,” said Doug Berger, the app’s general manager, in a statement.

articles.title: White House axes border wall game after Tetris pushback
articles.summary: The White House has removed its “Build the Wall” game from its MAGA-themed online arcade after The Tetris Company warned about possible copyright infringement. The block game closely resembled mechanics used in Tetris, with players stacking blocks to build a barrier alongside the southern border to prevent zombies and alien-like creatures from entering into the…
articles.body:
The White House has removed its “Build the Wall” game from its MAGA-themed online arcade after The Tetris Company warned about possible copyright infringement .

The block game closely resembled mechanics used in Tetris, with players stacking blocks to build a barrier alongside the southern border to prevent zombies and alien-like creatures from entering into the U.S.

The game was still available on the White House website Monday but was gone by Tuesday, according to archived versions of the site.

Tetris had publicly distanced itself from the game last week, saying it had nothing to do with its development.

“The Tetris Company was not involved in the creation of ‘Build the Wall,’” the company said in a statement, adding that it takes “copyright infringement very seriously.”

A Tetris spokesperson also told Variety last week that the White House had not received permission to use its brand or intellectual property and that it was reviewing the situation when asked whether the company may take legal action.

The White House launched its online arcade last week with five games based on President Trump’s policies ahead of the November midterms, each resembling popular existing games.

The four other games still remain on the White House website as of Wednesday.

Build the Wall was one of two immigration-themed games featured in the online arcade. Another called “Rio Run” mirrors the game Snake, in which an agent conducts “border patrol along the Rio Grande.”

The White House also did its own spin on the popular game Flappy Bird called “Flappy Bill,” in which a bald eagle carries legislation while jumping through obstacles along the National Mall.

“Trump Savings Tycoon” involves collecting money for Trump Accounts, while “Supply Line” — based on the administration’s Make America Healthy Again initiative — has players sort food.

articles.title: Knicks’ Jalen Brunson hosting ‘SNL’ season premiere
articles.summary: Live from New York, it’s Jalen Brunson! The New York Knicks star guard will host the season premiere of “Saturday Night Live” later this month as the NBC sketch comedy show returns for its 52nd run this fall. Brunson, who led the Knicks to their first NBA title in decades over the summer, will host…
articles.body:
The New York Knicks star guard will host the season premiere of “Saturday Night Live” later this month as the NBC sketch comedy show returns for its 52nd run this fall.

Brunson, who led the Knicks to their first NBA title in decades over the summer, will host the show on Sept. 26, the same night that will feature musical performances by K-pop group Katseye.

Brunson was named NBA Finals MVP for his performance against the San Antonio Spurs, capping a career-best season and ending the Knicks’ 53-year title drought. The team last won the NBA championship in 1973, two years before “SNL” debuted in 1975.

The Knicks captivated the nation with their title run earlier this year, with the front row of home games at Madison Square Garden packed with former “SNL” stars like Tina Fey, Ben Stiller and Tracy Morgan.

Also hosting “SNL” this fall will be actress Dakota Johnson on Oct. 3 and Shane Gillis on Oct. 10.

The show has been known in recent years for its political humor and skits poking fun at President Trump and other top U.S. officials. In June, Knicks owner James Dolan, a friend of the president who hosted him for Game 3 of the NBA finals, accepted an invitation for the team to visit the White House.

articles.title: 'Alien harboring' accusations fly as DC-area county spends taxpayer funds to blunt ICE
articles.summary: A Virginia county faces fire for a new policy providing taxpayer-funded grants to families of illegal immigrants whose breadwinner was deported by ICE.
articles.body: FIRST ON FOX: A Virginia county is under fire for a new policy providing taxpayer funds in the form of grants to families of illegal immigrants whose breadwinner was detained or deported by ICE. Arlington County, which sits just across the Potomac River from Washington, D.C., is not new to policies critics say interfere with DHS operations, as it previously caused outrage when the chair of the Arlington County board publicly suggested residents call police to report ICE sightings in January. "If you look at the alien harboring statute – do you do anything to encourage or induce people to either come illegally or that are illegally here to stay, that could be arguably a violation of the alien harboring statute?" former acting ICE Director Jonathan Fahey told Fox News Digital in a Wednesday interview. DOJ THREATENS TO CUT BILLIONS IN WELFARE FUNDING FROM STATES FOR FAILING TO REPORT ILLEGAL MIGRANTS "By giving money to people… the reasonable inference is that these people are also illegal, the money enables them to stay in the country illegally, because they lost their breadwinner," Fahey said. He said Arlington County Manager Mark Schwartz’s comments to ARLNow that many of the affected families are "unbanked" – or lack access to financial institutions which statutorily require identification to open deposit accounts – is itself a tell. TAXPAYER-FUNDED HOUSING FOR ILLEGAL IMMIGRANTS IN GOP'S CROSSHAIRS: 'IT'S GOT TO STOP' "That shows the county knows the money is going to be going to people that are illegally here and it will help them stay. So that's where I think the alien harboring statute comes into play," he said, adding the county shows "reckless disregard" for the fact their policies accommodate people in the country illegally. Arlington will start by setting aside $50,000 to be distributed through "social safety-net" ministry ArlingtonThrive in increments of up to $2,000 per affected family to cover basic needs and utilities, according to reports. The plan – which passed 4-0 with one board member absent – reportedly formed after a major ICE operation in Maryland and Virginia netted 1,328 illegal immigrant arrests, including the case of a man who ran from agents when confronted near the U.S. Air Force Memorial. Five regional federal Democrats sounded off afterward, endorsing an ensuing Arlington County Police investigation into the encounter between ICE and Jose Mejia Hernandez, who was reportedly tased and suffered a brain bleed. Fox News Digital reached out to Arlington County officials, including Chairman Matt de Ferranti, a Democrat from Rock Spring. "We are valuing the families of those that have been displaced and removed," he told local press. In January, de Ferranti warned Arlingtonians that county law prohibits its "public safety professionals" from "interfering with enforcement of federal immigration law," but that his suggestion to call 911 to report ICE sightings helps officials know agents are present and pivot to "pursu[ing] Arlington County’s law enforcement mission: preventing violence in our community." articles.title: Trump administration proposes excluding huge swath of immigrants from U.S. census
articles.summary: The Trump administration proposed on Wednesday changing the US census to include only U.S. citizens and permanent residents, a move that could significantly change how much political representation and federal funding each state receives.
articles.body: The Trump administration proposed on Wednesday changing the national census to include only U.S. citizens and permanent residents, a move that could significantly change how much political representation and federal funding each state receives. The U.S. Census Bureau submitted the proposal just over a year after President Donald Trump ordered its parent agency to craft a new census that would block immigrants in the U.S. illegally from being counted. The bureau will conduct the next full census in 2030. The proposed rule changes would exclude even more immigrants from the census, such as those in the U.S. on a temporary lawful basis. The proposed changes would also eliminate parts of the questionnaire that seek information on race or ethnicity, which have been included since the first census in 1790. The proposal is open to public comment for 30 days. Demography experts and civil rights advocates warn that both changes could warp the data used for drawing congressional and state legislative districts, enforcing anti-discrimination law and allocating federal funds for public services. The effort could have “earth-shattering” effects, leaving cities and states that have relatively high immigrant populations with insufficient federal aid and political representation, said Meeta Anand, senior director of the census and data equity program at the Leadership Conference on Civil and Human Rights. Census data “undergirds so much of our democracy and our society,” Anand said. “So you’ll start seeing a very inaccurate picture of our country, and then we’re making political decisions, business decisions, investment decisions based on data that are flawed.” The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Trump has long decried the fact that immigrants living in the U.S. illegally are included in the census, which is used to determine how many seats each state gets in the U.S. House of Representatives and state legislative districts. In his first term, Trump tried to add a citizenship question to the 2020 census but was blocked by the U.S. Supreme Court, which ruled that the federal government had given a “contrived” rationale. The U.S. Constitution’s 14th Amendment calls for political representatives to be apportioned based on “the whole number of persons in each State.” The administration’s effort to omit immigrants in the U.S. illegally and temporary immigrants from the U.S. census comes amid its wider crackdown on both legal and illegal immigration across the country. The Justice Department warned on September 2 that states could lose billions of dollars ‌in welfare funding if they do not report all immigrants whom state agencies know to be in the country illegally.

articles.title: Lindsay Clancy attorney will ask for jury to be sequestered in new trial
articles.summary: Prosecutors have yet to make a decision on retrying Lindsay Clancy after a mistrial was declared in the case.
articles.body:
Editor’s Note : This story contains discussions of child abuse that may be disturbing. Reader discretion is advised. If you suspect a child is being abused, find out how to report it in your state here . To connect with a counselor, you can call the National Child Abuse Hotline at 1-800-422-4253.

( NewsNation ) — Defense Attorney Kevin Reddington said he would request the jury be sequestered in a new trial for Lindsay Clancy .

Speaking to reporters, Reddington said he would ask the judge but noted that sequestration isn’t common anymore.

“I’ll request it, we’ll see what the judge does,” he said.

When a jury is sequestered, they are housed in a hotel for the duration of the trial, not allowed to access news media or coverage of the case. Judges may confiscate electronic devices like cell phones or laptops, or may monitor the use of such devices so jurors cannot access outside information.

A judge declared a mistrial in the Clancy case after a five-week trial, when jurors failed to reach an agreement after seven days of deliberation.

Clancy was facing murder charges in the deaths of her three young children. Prosecutors argued she planned to commit the crime and knew what she was doing, while Reddington told the court his client was suffering from postpartum psychosis and not criminally responsible for her actions.

The jury, made up of nine women and three men, had 11 members who found Clancy not guilty by reason of insanity and one holdout who found her guilty.

The case attracted national attention, sparking conversations about postpartum psychosis and sharply divided opinions on Clancy’s guilt.

One woman, Dawn Light , is facing charges of intimidation after allegedly taking photos of jurors exiting the courthouse.

Jury sequestration is not often used because of the high costs , logistical difficulties and burden on jurors who have to be away from their loved ones for the duration of the trial. Instead, jurors are typically instructed by a judge to avoid media coverage and to not discuss the case with anyone.

However, juries in high-profile cases, like the OJ Simpson trial, have been sequestered due to the intense amount of media coverage that might make it difficult for jurors to avoid outside information.

While Reddington said he would ask about sequestration, he also told reporters that he didn’t think it would make much of a difference and that he didn’t think the jurors were influenced by outside factors.

“I don’t believe any of these people violated the judge’s orders; they were honest, they were hardworking,” he said.

Prosecutors have not yet made a decision on retrying Clancy.

articles.body:
President Trump said Wednesday he believes the U.S. war with Iran will end “immediately” after November’s midterm elections.

“I think the war is going to end immediately after the election,” Trump told reporters at Joint Base Andrews en route to the Republican midterm convention in Dallas.

“They can’t hold out any longer,” he continued. “They’re desperate to try and affect the election so that we can get a nice, weak group of people in there, and leave them alone and let them have their nuclear weapon.”

Trump made the prediction when asked at Joint Base Andrews whether he expects negotiations with Iran to resume.

“We’re not looking for it, to be honest,” Trump responded. “Originally, I wanted to make a deal. We’re so far down the line. We have very little country left.”

“Yes, a negotiation could possibly happen, but it’s not something we’re looking at,” he added.

The president’s comments come after Iran said Wednesday that it targeted 10 ships near the Strait of Hormuz, including two U.S. vessels and eight oil tankers. Those strikes followed the U.S. destroying five Iranian oil tankers Tuesday.

“We’ve knocked out nine of their ships. I would say that the attacks are caused by us, and you’re going to see a lot more,” Trump told reporters Wednesday.

Trump’s approval rating has dropped to 33 percent, according to the latest Reuters/Ipsos survey , with the Iran war and rising prices as key factors, causing concerns among Republicans as November approaches.

articles.title: Trump administration fires prosecutor in dropped case against politically linked Indian billionaire
articles.summary: A federal prosecutor who had been assigned to the now-defunct case against a politically-linked Indian billionaire has been fired by the Trump administration, two people familiar with the firing tell NBC News.
articles.body: WASHINGTON — A federal prosecutor who had been assigned to the now-defunct case against a politically linked Indian billionaire has been fired by the Trump administration, two people familiar with the firing tell NBC News. The prosecutor, who had been with the Justice Department’s Fraud Section in Washington, was one of two who previously asked to withdraw from the Gautam Adani case two days after Principal Associate Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter moved in May to dismiss the case against Adani. Adani was charged in November 2024 in connection with an alleged scheme to defraud U.S. investors and pay off Indian government officials to win a bid to develop the country’s largest solar power plant. He called the accusations baseless. Adani pledged to invest billions of dollars in the U.S., and Democratic lawmakers raised questions of a quid pro quo with the Trump administration to avoid prosecution. The federal judge hearing the case ordered Adani to explain whether any deal was made in connection with the government’s significant reversal. He denied it, and so did the Justice Department. U.S. District Judge Nicholas Garaufis of the Eastern District of New York eventually agreed to toss the case against Adani, though he blasted the Trump administration’s “highly unusual” conduct. The prosecutor’s firing came a month later, the people said. The Trump administration has fired numerous federal employees without explanation, beyond citing Trump’s executive powers in letters, which Justice Department alumni have come to refer to as “Article II letters,” referring to a clause of the U.S. Constitution. A spokesperson for the Eastern District of New York declined to comment. The prosecutor did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Last week, Garaufis let stand some counts against some of Adani’s co-defendants, saying the Trump administration had “not provided sufficient factual information to support the stated reasons” for dismissing the charges. Adani had pledged to invest billions of dollars in the United States but said in a sworn statement filed in July that he was “not aware of any agreement involving any person or entity exchanging anything for the dismissal of the indictment.” An email from May from U.S. Attorney Joseph Nocella referenced a slide deck presentation from Adani’s defense team that included a proposal to invest $10 billion in the United States, and Nocella wrote that the proposal was “categorically rejected” by the office. The Justice Department has defended the decision to forgo its case against Adani, with McCotter saying the case was “indefensible” and that he “would have sought dismissal of the securities charges regardless of any mentions of investments, regardless of whether the civil case (or any other matter) was settled or otherwise resolved.” An attorney for Adani couldn’t be reached for comment about the prosecutor’s firing.

An emergency inflatable slide on the Qatari-gifted Air Force One was deployed at Joint Base Andrews before President Trump departed for the Republican midterm convention in Dallas on Wednesday.

The slide was inflated onto the tarmac from the door on the right-hand side, opposite the door that Trump usually uses to enter the plane, according to the White House press pool traveling with the president.

Trump unusually remained inside of Marine One for more than 20 minutes after landing at Joint Base Andrews, as the slide was deployed.

When asked by reporters about the slide, Trump told reporters, “They want to make sure everything works perfectly.”

The development comes as the new Qatari-gifted jet has come under heavy scrutiny over security concerns around its defense capabilities in recent months.

Last month, The Washington Post reported that Trump secretly departed the NATO summit in Turkey in July using an alternate military aircraft amid a security threat from Iran. Trump had arrived at the summit on the Qatari-gifted jet.

Prior to the bombshell report, Trump announced in Turkey that he would be using the old Air Force One to leave the summit and board the new jet in the United Kingdom. He claimed the plane shuffle would allow troops stationed overseas to see the newly renovated jet.

Trump was seen boarding the old Air Force One in Ankara but was secretly shuttled by Secret Service in a catering truck to a military aircraft, according to the Post report.

articles.title: Trump says he’d consider pardoning Michael Cohen

articles.body:
President Trump said Friday he would consider pardoning attorney Michael Cohen, while complaining about how the legal system treated his former fixer.

Trump was asked about whether he would pardon Cohen, who was the star witness in the 2024 New York hush money trial, since he recanted everything he said.

“It was illegal what they did,” Trump said before boarding Air Force One to Dallas. “What they put him through was incredible.”

“What they did to Michael Cohen was a disgrace,” continued. “They forced him to say things that he didn’t want to say and that he didn’t believe. And I appreciate that at least he came out, although late, he came out and rectified the situation.”

Cohen has not recanted his testimony, though he and Trump have made peace. Cohen has also said he felt pressured by prosecutors to testify against the president.

On the pardon, Trump said, “If everything is checking out, it’s something I would consider.”

Last week, Trump wrote on social media that Cohen had “fully RECANTED his testimony.”

“He was ‘pressured’ and ‘coerced’ to say things that were not true,” Trump wrote on Truth Social. “I would like to thank Michael for having the Wisdom and Courage to step forward and do the right thing!”

“His Act of Bravery is a Great Credit to the Justice System in New York City and State,” he continued. “I am sure it was not easy for him! Now we are asking that any remnant of those Politically Weaponized Cases against me be immediately terminated and dismissed.”

Cohen was Trump’s former personal attorney who turned into the star witness for the criminal hush money payment case against Trump in New York in 2024. He admitted in court to facilitating payments to porn actor Stormy Daniels to cover up an alleged affair before the 2016 presidential election.

Cohen has since worked to reconcile with Trump. He told John Catsimatidis and Rita Cosby on WABC’s “Cats & Cosby” radio show in July that he had gotten a text from the president about six months ago.

He had Trump on his radio show on WABC last month.

The president has suggested Cohen was “forced” to testify against him in the 2024 case. He told Cohen during the radio show that the government was “weaponized” against him.

“There were plenty of others too, and it’s a disgrace,” he said. “I think it’s so amazing that you came out, and you told the story, and people respect you for doing it.”

Cohen told CNN in August he sent a written pardon application to the White House but has not spoken directly to Trump about it.

articles.title: Lewandowski pushes back on ‘politically driven’ Wall Street Journal report
articles.summary: Former Trump adviser Corey Lewandowski on Tuesday pushed back on a recent Wall Street Journal article alleging he controlled billions of dollars of Department of Homeland Security (DHS) contracts, accusing the news outlet’s reporting of being “politically driven.” The DHS designated Lewandowski as a “special government employee” allowed to carry out private business for the…
articles.body:
Former Trump adviser Corey Lewandowski on Tuesday pushed back on a recent Wall Street Journal article alleging he controlled billions of dollars of Department of Homeland Security (DHS) contracts, accusing the news outlet’s reporting of being “politically driven.”

The DHS designated Lewandowski as a “special government employee” allowed to carry out private business for the department. It was in this capacity that the Journal claimed he pitched government services to Qatari and Emirati officials.

A representative for the former adviser denied to the Journal that Lewandowski “sought contracts with foreign governments,” adding he “adamantly denies ever demanding any payment or compensation from any potential, former, or current government contractor or seeking … contracts with foreign governments while volunteering his time with DHS.”

“This latest Wall Street Journal story, a once great publication, is today just another example of the kind of anonymous-source, politically driven reporting that Americans have seen time and again,” Lewandowski wrote on the social platform X .

He added that he was “tremendously proud of” his “work as a volunteer in advancing this administration’s agenda,” writing in a separate post that the Journal’s story was “fiction.”

“On the week of the 25th Anniversary of 9/11 you would think the WSJ would be more interested in how our homeland has become secure as opposed to the innuendo fake news story they published today,” he continued.

The Journal cited unnamed sources who claimed Lewandowski approached officials from Qatar and the United Arab Emirates offering to help with issues falling under DHS purview, including visas. Some of these officials were reportedly taken aback by the offers and declined.

Lewandowski’s role at the DHS gave him authority to decide the use of “large amounts of recently appropriated billions of dollars.” He was an adviser to, and had a personal relationship with, former DHS Secretary Kristi Noem before she was ousted from her role due to excessive spending allegations.

House Democrats asked the DHS’s Office of Inspector General to open an investigation into Lewandowski earlier this year, accusing him of mismanagement and corruption.

They cited a separate Journal article claiming Lewandowski urged Noem to ditch some of the DHS’s long-term contracts in favor of newer agreements, posing challenges to grant applicants.

The reporting prompted lawmakers to urge the DHS to rescind the $100,000 approval policy and return to the prior approval threshold, “given the clear risk of mismanagement, confusion, and self-dealing.”

Last month, Sen. Maggie Hassan (D-N.H.) pressed the DHS for interim findings and other records from its investigation into Lewandowski.

“The allegations against Mr. Lewandowski, if true, indicate significant corruption, abuse of taxpayer funds, and flagrant conflicts of interest that require Congressional investigation based on a comprehensive record of his tenure at DHS,” wrote Hassan, a senior member of the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, in a letter to DHS Under Secretary for Management Brian Cavanaugh.
