articles.title: Florida sues Netflix, alleges streamer tracked children after promising families privacy
articles.summary: Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier alleges Netflix secretly harvested children's behavioral data to build the ad business it vowed never to create.
articles.body: Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier sued Netflix on Wednesday, accusing the streaming giant of misleading subscribers by promising an ad-free, privacy-focused service while secretly collecting years of behavioral data — including from children's profiles — to build the advertising business it long insisted it would never create. The 66-page lawsuit alleges Netflix built its brand by assuring consumers that paying a monthly subscription meant they could avoid the surveillance-driven advertising model used by other major technology companies. Instead, Florida alleges Netflix quietly collected extensive user data before launching its ad-supported platform in November 2022. "Netflix told Florida families they could pay a monthly fee to escape Big Tech surveillance. That was false," Uthmeier said in a news release announcing the lawsuit. "Netflix collected detailed data on children and families, designed its product to keep kids watching, and then commercialized that information to launch the advertising business it promised never to build. Parents, not corporate executives, direct the upbringing of their children. Netflix should expect to be held accountable." The complaint points to repeated public statements from Netflix executives who touted the company as different from advertising-supported competitors. Among them, the lawsuit cites former CEO Reed Hastings, who said during a 2020 earnings call that Netflix was "not integrating everybody's data," adding, "We don't collect anything," and describing the streaming service as "the safe respite" from companies that exploit users through advertising. WASHINGTON POST FACES CLASS-ACTION LAWSUIT ALLEGING 'SURVEILLANCE PRICING' OF SUBSCRIBERS Florida alleges those assurances were misleading because Netflix built what the lawsuit describes as a massive behavioral-data operation that records how subscribers use the platform. According to the complaint, Netflix tracks billions of user interactions, including what subscribers watch, search for, pause, rewind, skip and abandon, along with information about their devices and locations. The state alleges Netflix uses that information to improve its recommendation systems and support its advertising business. The lawsuit places particular emphasis on Netflix's Kids Profiles, which the company markets as dedicated spaces designed for children. Florida alleges Netflix encouraged parents to create children's profiles by describing them as "Great for kids" and a child's "own space" while continuing to collect and analyze children's viewing behavior through the same telemetry systems used for adult accounts. PARENTS PUSH CONGRESS TO ACT ON KIDS' ONLINE SAFETY AFTER JURIES FIND META AND YOUTUBE LIABLE FOR HARM Florida also accuses Netflix of using so-called "dark patterns" to keep viewers engaged. The complaint alleges autoplay, which is enabled by default on Kids Profiles, is intentionally designed to extend viewing sessions, increase binge watching and generate additional behavioral data, particularly from children. The state further alleges Netflix expanded into the advertising business it once rejected by allowing advertisers and advertising technology companies to use subscriber data for audience targeting and campaign measurement after launching its ad-supported tier in November 2022. The lawsuit accuses Netflix of violating the Florida Deceptive and Unfair Trade Practices Act and the Florida Digital Bill of Rights. Among other claims, Florida alleges Netflix unlawfully shared sensitive personal data collected from children without obtaining the consent required under state law. MARYLAND MOVES TO BAN SURVEILLANCE PRICING IN GROCERY STORES Uthmeier is asking the court to permanently block the alleged practices, order Netflix to delete data the state says was deceptively collected from Floridians, stop using historical subscriber data to support its advertising business, purge behavioral data collected through Kids Profiles, prohibit the use of alleged dark-pattern designs and impose civil penalties authorized under Florida law. 'WHY WOULD HE DO THIS TO US?': ONE CRUCIAL TRUMP DECISION IS HURTING HIS BASE, REPUBLICANS WARN And midterm elections are more often than not a referendum against the party in power. Scott, however, believed that Republicans were going to "actually have a good cycle," and maintain control of the Senate. "The reason is we have a better message and we have great candidates," Scott said. "If you look at our Senate candidates, I mean, how would you like to be out and defend [Abdul] El-Sayed's record of being antisemitic and hating this country." Much of the purpose of the convention, Scott acknowledged, was to remind voters that while his name isn’t explicitly on the ballot, the midterm elections were all about President Donald Trump. articles.body:
Congress’s official ethics watchdog has cleared Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-Minn.) of misconduct related to inflated financial filings, according to the office of the Minnesota Democrat.

The Office of Congressional Conduct (OCC) “delivered an overwhelming vote to dismiss any allegations against the Congresswoman,” an Omar spokesperson said Wednesday in a statement.

“From day one, we have been clear: the Congresswoman is not a millionaire,” the spokesperson said.

The OCC, an independent bipartisan panel, had launched an investigation into Omar after she submitted financial disclosures last year claiming that assets she owned jointly with her husband were worth between $6 million and $30 million.

The figures marked a sharp increase above those Omar claimed just a year earlier, and they sparked an outcry from Republicans on Capitol Hill who demanded an investigation into the source of Omar’s wealth.

President Trump piled on, accusing Omar of profiting illegally from a multi-billion-dollar fraud scheme plaguing Minnesota’s social services programs — allegations Omar strongly denied.

In April, Omar amended her financial disclosures, sharply reducing the value of her claimed assets. She blamed the inflated figures in the initial disclosure on an accounting error.

The filings caught the eye of top Republicans in the Capitol, including Rep. James Comer (R-Ky.), the chairman of the House Oversight Committee, who sought records from Omar’s husband earlier in the year.

Omar, a former Somali refugee and one of the first Muslims to serve in Congress, has long been a target of Republicans. She says the controversy surrounding her finances has been manufactured by Trump and other GOP lawmakers as part of that longer feud. On Wednesday, Omar’s office said the OCC’s dismissal of the case validates that position.

“This vote clearly underscores that the Congresswoman did nothing wrong, and attempts by the far right to manufacture controversy and distract from the facts are pathetic and nothing more than a desperate distraction from their own failures,” the spokesperson said.

The news of the OCC’s decision was first reported on Wednesday by The Wall Street Journal .

A spokesman for the OCC declined to comment.

articles.body:
President Trump hit back at a question Thursday over why some Republican candidates were skipping the midterm GOP convention in Dallas, saying there isn’t room for everyone.

Trump said, “everybody wants to come,” to the convention and questioned the reporter, Mary Bruce of ABC, on what outlet she was with.

He bashed her outlet before going on to say that the reason some weren’t attending the convention is “we don’t have room for 500 politicians.”

“We have room for the ones that have a close race, if they’re slightly behind or slightly ahead or tied,” he said. “But we don’t have room for people that are 35 points up and don’t need to be there.”

“We said stay back and campaign,” he continued. “Every politician that we’ve wanted to be there is there.”

The midterm convention is set for Thursday and Friday. Some Republicans are skipping the event , which has been branded as a “Trump-a-palooza.”

Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine) is one of the most prominent figures who has decided to skip the convention amid facing a tough reelection battle.

Sen. Mike Rounds (R-S.D.) has also said he will skip and spend time with his constituents. Sen. Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska) will also be missing the convention.

Reps. Maria Elvira Salazar (Fla.), Tom Barrett (Mich.), Juan Ciscomani (Ariz.), Zach Nunn (Iowa) and David Valadao (Calif.) have also decided to miss the convention, CNN reported.

The convention has sparked mixed emotions among Republicans who point to the possible political risk of being closely tied to Trump before the election amid high costs and the Iran war.
